searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Exploring Network information and Assigning Static IP Addresses to your Virtual Machines​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Right now, our virtual machines are all set to receive their IP addresses automatically via DHCP from the host OS. We are going to change them all to use a static IP address so that their IP address never changes.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Finding IP information on Server1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Begin by powering on and logging in to Server1.Click the blue windows icon at the bottom of the screen, type "cmd", and press "Enter". A Windows Command Prompt window will appear.Enter the following command in the command prompt:  ipconfig   Notice the IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask, and Default Gateway fields. What does this information tell us?  Now enter:  ipconfig /all   Notice that we are given a lot more information. So what are we looking for?  There are several pieces of information here that are useful to us. The result of the first command we ran gives us the IP address and its subnet mask, as well as the default gateway (or the router/device it looks to in order to send data outside of the local network.  The second command gives us more details about the networking information associate with this machine. Specifically for us, we are interested in the DHCP information and the DNS information.  The DNS server is the server that is providing translations for IP addresses to Fully Qualified Domain Names and vice versa. We will be creating our own DNS server later on in this lab.  The DHCP server is the server that is providing this machine with an IP address. When a computer with DHCP enabled comes online, it reaches out to the network via a broadcast to find a DHCP server. If it finds one, the two machines perform a DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) exchange and the DHCP server assigns an IP address to the machine that has just come online. The computer will keep this IP address for as long as it has a lease for it. You can also find the lease information in the output that we got from the "ipconfig /all" command. Using the two lease time stamps provided, we can determine how long the DHCP server has leased this IP to this machine. When we are done with part 1 here, we will change this machine to use a static IP address instead of a DHCP assigned one.  Take a look at the "Lease Obtained" and "Lease Expires" lines in the output of "ipconfig /all". Now enter:  ipconfig /release   What happened?  Run "ipconfig /all" again and take a look at the "Lease Obtained" line. What changed?Now enter:  ipconfig /renew   What happened?  Run "ipconfig /all" again and take a look at the "Lease Obtained" line. What happened?  The "ipconfig /release" and "ipconfig /renew" commands do similar things. The "/release" option releases the DHCP assigned IP address from the machine. The "/renew" option does the same thing but then also immediately asks for a new one. So why did Server1 still have a DHCP IP address when we ran "ipconfig /all" after running "ipconfig /release"?. The short answer is: VMware. There are many small factors that differ between actual physical networks and virtual networks and this is one of them. You will discover several others as you proceed through this program.  Either way, it is important to remember the distinction between those two commands.  Keep in mind that right now, VMware is effectively acting as the default gateway, DNS server, and DHCP server. Due to the virtual nature of our network, VMware and the host OS control all of these networking services (again, another intricacy of a virtual network).  Now let's do some basic network testing.  Enter "ping google.com" into the command prompt. You should see 4 replies appear. This tells you that your Server1 machine was able to contact the website "google.com" (probably hosted on a 142.x.x.x IP address). Pings are a useful tool to test network connectivity to devices that are on both our internal network and networks external to our own.Try the following 3 commands:  ping localhost ping loopback ping 127.0.0.1   What were the outputs of these commands? What were you pinging?  The loopback address (referenced as 127.0.0.1 or localhost or loopback) is a special IP address that is on all systems. It represents the system that is running it so when you ping it you are having Server1 ping itself. This may not sound super useful (and with pings it isn't) but it is very useful when testing network services that the server is providing. We will be using it later in this lab.  Now try:  ping -n 10 google.com   What changed about the ping output? There are times when network stability cannot be guaranteed or ascertained. So you may send out a ping and the first 4 pings fail but later pings may succeed. This is not typical but there are times when running extended pings can be useful.  Finally, try:  ping -t google.com   What happened? How many pings are used? Press Ctrl+C when you get tired of watching pings.  Now that you have a general idea of how to get basic network information, we are going to change our network a little so that we have better control over it and so that we can begin to work with network services.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 2: Windows Firewall and Packet Filtering​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Earlier in this lab, you used pings from Server1 to test connectivity with the outside world. However, that was when the IP addressed was still being assigned by DHCP. Let's see what happens now that we have statically assigned an IP address to our VMs.  Power on Server1, log in, and bring up the command prompt.Confirm that your IP address and subnet mask are still 10.10.xxx.10 and 255.255.255.0.If they are, try pinging google.  ping google.com   Your ping should fail (likely with a "request could not find host..." error).  The primary reason is that Server1 does not have a default gateway. We intentionally left that configuration blank. Because of this, Server1 does not know where to send data if the target is not on its local network. Server1, Server2, and Client1 have all been configured in such a way that they can no longer connect with the Internet or anything external to their local network. However, they can still connect to each other. Let's try that next.  Power on Server2.Log in and navigate to the Powershell command line.Confirm that your IP address and subnet mask are still 10.10.xxx.20 and 255.255.255.0.Try to ping Server1 from Server 2:  ping 10.10.xxx.10   What happened? Your ping requests should have timed out. The problem now does not have to do with our network setup. Our problem now is the Windows Firewall. You will go into more detail regarding packet filtering and firewalls (both Windows and others) in other courses but right now our problem is that the Windows Firewall is blocking our ping requests. This will happen on all 3 VMs because all 3 have Windows Firewall running and the firewall will not allow ICMP traffic (the protocol used by pings) to get through. Let's fix this.  Still in Server2, run the following command:  New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings" -Direction Inbound -Protocol ICMPv4 -IcmpType 8 -Action Allow   Verify that the rule has been added successfully:  Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings"   Switch over to Server 1, open Powershell as an Administrator and run the same commands:  New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings" -Direction Inbound -Protocol ICMPv4 -IcmpType 8 -Action Allow Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings"   Now power on Client 1, open Powershell as an Administrator and run the same commands:  New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings" -Direction Inbound -Protocol ICMPv4 -IcmpType 8 -Action Allow Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow Pings"   We can now try to ping Server1 and Server2 from Client1:  ping 10.10.xxx.10 ping 10.10.xxx.20   Switch back over to Server1 and ping Server2 and Client1 from Server1:  ping 10.10.xxx.20 ping 10.10.xxx.100   Screenshot 4: Take a screenshot showing successful pings from Server1 to Server2 and Client1  Screenshot 5: Take a screenshot showing successful pings from Client1 to Server1 and Server2  Now that we have full connectivity between our VMs, we can start working on a few basic network services.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 3: Configuring DNS and IIS​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: In lab 3, we installed the DNS and IIS roles onto our Server1 but we did not make any changes to those services. We are going to use these services to create a small, simple webpage that will be accessible from Client1.  Keep in mind that in order for this to work, Server1 must have a static IP address because it is hosting these services. The IP address cannot change otherwise other computers would not be able to reliably find it. This principle is the same whether we are talking about finding a web server on a tiny little network like ours or a website on the Internet.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Configuring IIS on Server1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: First, we will make a small change to the default webpage that comes with IIS, just so we can differentiate it from the default one.  In Server Manager, from the Tools pull-down menu (in the upper-right corner of the Server Manager), find and run "Internet Information Services (IIS) Manager".In the left pane, expand the tree under your server name until "Default Web Site" appears.Right-click on the Default Web Site and choose Explore.From the new Window you can modify your starter web site by opening the file iisstart (the HTML file, NOT the PNG file) in Notepad. You will be editing HTML code in this file. To make a basic modification to the site, change the title of the page by modifying the text that appears between the <title> tags to include your name. You may also make any other modifications you like (not required). Save and exit the file.To view your web page locally, open a web browser, and type 127.0.0.1 in the browser address bar. (Remember, 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address and not your actual IP address.) The default IIS webpage should appear (an image with a bunch of blue squares and "Welcome" written in different languages), and the tab title should have your changes. As long as you can see your name in the tab title you have edited the HTML file correctly.  MAYBE USE AI HERE TO MAKE A SIMPLE HTML PAGE??

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Configuring DNS on Server1​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Now that our webpage is updated, we need to set up DNS so that we can access that webpage using a Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) instead of an IP address. To accomplish this, we will be mapping the IP address of our Server1 to a domain.  In Server Manager, from the Tools pull-down menu, select DNS. The DNS Manager will appear, displaying your server name, which should be your SenecaID (not a name that starts with WIN) in both the left and right panes.Expand the tree for your server [>], then right-click Forward Lookup Zone, and select New Zone.Click Next. Make the zone a Primary Zone. Click Next.Type in a zone name for your web server. Use your Seneca ID + .com (ex. hheim.com).Click Next and allow the wizard to create the zone file for you. Click Next. Ensure "Do not allow dynamic updates" is selected. Click Next and click Finish.Expand the Forward Lookup Zone in the left pane until you see your zone name (senecaID.com). Right-click on your new domain name and choose to Add New Host. The New Host dialog box will appear.Enter "server1" in the "Host" field and add the IP address of your web server (the IP address that was manually configured for your installation of Windows Server on Server1) to the IP address field. You do not need to create a pointer record.Click Add Host, and then OK when you get your success message. Click Done to close the window.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Testing our Web Server​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Before we move on to testing our configurations, take a moment to recall how we configured Server1, Server2, and Client1's network settings. In addition to the IP address and subnet mask, we also entered in a preferred DNS IP address. This was the IP address of Server1 (10.10.xxx.10). What this means is that all 3 VMs will look to Server1 to resolve IP addresses to FQDNs and vice versa. Now that we have created a host (A) record, if we try to access the FQDN via a web browser we should connect to the Web Page that is being hosted on Server1 since its FQDN matches its IP address in the host (A) record.  To test the new domain name locally, open your web browser and type the domain name you entered above (http://server1.senecaID.com), in the address bar field. Your webpage should display as it did before. This proves that your DNS Server (that you just configured) is resolving the name (server1.senecaID.com) to the correct IP address to find the web page on your web server. (Note - make sure you specify http and not https. It will want to default to https.)  If your webpage does not appear, check your Preferred DNS settings on Server1 to make sure you have entered the correct IP address (10.10.xxx.10) and that you created the host (A) record correctly.  Now let's test to see if we can connect to this web server from Client1.  Log in to Client1, open a web browser and enter "http://server1.senecaid.com"  You should see the same web page you saw on Server1 and can confirm it is the same page if you see your name in the tab title.  If your webpage does not appear, check your Preferred DNS settings on Client1 to make sure you have entered the correct IP address (10.10.xxx.10). searchDocs.title: Part 4: Adding Authentication to our Web page​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: Our example in this lab is very simple and straightforward. We mapped the IP address of our web server (Server1, 10.10.xxx.10) to the FQDN http://server1.senecaid.com. Also, this web page is only accessible on our local virtual network. We are not letting the outside world access it. Only our own VMs can access it so we aren't really worried about security at this point. However, security is ALWAYS something we need to worry about in the real world. So we are going to add a level of it to our web page by requiring authentication to access the website.  Using Server Manager on Server1, click IIS in the left pane. Your server name should appear in the right pane. Right-click the server and select Add Roles and Features from the menu.Select Next a couple of times until you reach the screen with the roles displayed.Scroll down to your Web Server Role and expand it [>] to see the available roles and features.Select Web Server. Then select Security. Place a checkmark next to "Basic Authentication".Click Next, Next, and Install. Close the window once the installation completes.Open the IIS Manager (Tools >> IIS). Expand the tree to find your Default Web Site.Double-click on the Authentication icon in the middle pane.Disable Anonymous Authentication and Enable Basic Authentication.  We have now turned basic authentication on but we still need to create the credentials that will be allowed to access the web page.  Open a Command Prompt as an Administrator and type the following command:  net user webuser P@ssw0rd /ADD   This creates a new user account on the server, called "webuser" and the account has a password of "P@ssw0rd". 4. Test your website again on Client1 (you may have to refresh your web page). What is the difference now?  Screenshot 7: Take a screenshot showing the authentication window appearing on the web page on Client1  You should be able to use your new webuser account to login to gain access to the website.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 4: Connecting from Client1 to Server2 using RDP​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 4: Introduction to Windows Networking and Network Services
searchDocs.content: The last thing we are going to do is enable Remote Desktop on Server2 so that we can connect to it from our Client1 VM. This is very useful as we generally do not log in directly to Server Core machines. As a security measure, we stick to remote connecions.  Log into Server 2 and find "Remote desktop" on the Sconfig screen. It should be number 7. Enter "7".Enter "E" to enable it and then enter "2".Reboot your Server2.When Server2 comes back up, do not log in. Switch over to Client1.On Client1, press the Windows key, type "run" and press "Enter".Enter "MSTSC" and hit "Enter". The "Remote Desktop Connection" window will appear.Enter "10.10.xxx.20" (Server2) into the "Computer" field and click "Connect".You will be asked for your Server2 credentials. Enter them.Click "Yes" when it asks you about a certificate.You should successfully connect to your Server2 from Client1 via RDP. searchDocs.title: Part 3: Creating Your MST100 Working Directories and Storing the ISOs Inside​

DO NOT LOSE THIS KEY. DO NOT SHARE THIS KEY WITH ANYONE. You may want to also store a copy of this key in your OneDrive just in case your hard drive is rendered unusable.  Now you have your ISOs and security key in the right place and you have your directories ready to install to in next week's lab.

searchDocs.title: Part 1-2: Windows Server 2025 GUI Post-Installation Tasks​
searchDocs.pageTitle: Lab 2: Installing Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 Virtual Machines
searchDocs.content: Now that our Server1 is installed, there are a few things we need to do to prepare it for our labs. We are going to ensure our Time Zone is correct and we are going to name our system appropriately. Then we are going to make sure our system is completely updated. FInally, we will confirm internet connectivity and download a better web browser.  Log into your Server1. To use Ctrl+Alt+Del in your VM, click "VM" in VMware and select "Send Ctrl+Alt+Del".You should be met with the Server Manager Dashboard. searchDocs.title: Investigation 3: The Windows Registry​
searchDocs.content: The Windows Registry is a critically important part of any Microsoft Windows operating system. It is essentially a database that stores all computer, system, application and user settings. More importantly, it is referenced by Windows for just about every operation that can occur on the OS. It cannot be overstated just how important the Registry is and how important it is to not mess around in it.  In this next section we are going to mess around in the Registry.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Exporting Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Before we go in and start changing things, we are going to learn how to backup up parts of the registry. We are not going to change anything critical in the Registry but (as is the case with any configuration on any system) it is always a good idea to backup your default settings. That way, if you break something, you can always revert to the backup.  Entries in the registry are called "Keys". They vary widely in structure and function but they can all be backed up the same way. We are going to be modifying the key that controls the legal notice when logging into Windows so we are going to back up that key along with the entire location in which it sits.  Power on Server1 and log in.Click the blue Windows button at the bottom of the screen and type "run" and hit "Enter".The "Run" dialogue box will appear. Enter "regedit" and click "OK". The Registry Editor window will appear. Note: Take extra care when navigating the Registry. There are many directories that appear as duplicates down different paths of the registry directory tree and you want to make sure you are in the right place before making any changes. Changes made in the wrong place can end in disastrous results.Navigate to the following path in the Registry Editor: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Microsoft\ Windows\ CurrentVersion\ policies\ systemIf you are in the right place you will see the "legalnoticecaption" and "legalnoticetext" keys. Click "File" in the top-left of the Registry Editor window and then click "Export".Name your backup "RegistryLegalNotice.reg" and save it to the C: drive.Using the File Explorer, navigate to your C: drive.  Screenshot 5: Take a screenshot showing your RegistryLegalNotice.reg file in the C: drive directory.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Modifying Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Now that we have a backup, we can proceed to modify the legal keys.  Back in the Registry Editor, double click on the legalnoticecaption key. Enter the value as "This is a Secure PC" and click "OK".Double click on the legalnoticetext key. Enter the value as "Only authorized users can log into this computer and use this network. Non-authorized users will be recorded and prosecuted." and click "OK".Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Close the Registry Editor and reboot Server1.  Once it reboots and you go to log in, notice that you will now see your legal messages.  Screenshot 6: Take a screenshot showing these messages before you log in.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Adding Registry Keys​
searchDocs.content: Keys can be modified but we can also add keys for new functionality or if keys are missing.  Log back into Server1 and open the Registry Editor again.Navigate to the following path (BE CAREFUL and double check where you are!): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Microsoft\ Windows NT\ CurrentVersionIf you are in the right place you will see the several keys with "Build" in the name at the top of the list.Right-click in the white space where the keys are stored and click "New">>"String Value".Name it "RegisteredOwner",press "Enter", then double click it and enter your name for its value.Again, right-click in the white space where the keys are stored and click "New">>"String Value".Name it "RegisteredOrganization",press "Enter", then double click it and enter "Seneca Polytechnic" for its value.Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Hit Winkey+R on your keyboard (a nice shortcut to bring up the "Run" dialogue box). Enter "winver.exe" and click "OK". The "About Windows" window should appear and your Name and Organization will be listed at the bottom.  Screenshot 7: Take a screenshot showing your name and organization in the "About Windows" window.  Let's add another key. This time we will add something that is actually useful on our system.  Navigate to the following path in the Registry Editor (CAUTION! THIS IS A DIFFERENT PATH THAN THE LAST ONE!): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ SOFTWARE\ Policies\ Microsoft\ Windows NTThere should be only one key here (the Default key). Right-click in the white space and click "New">>"Key". You will see a new path entry on the left side of the screen appear inside "Windows NT".Rename it to "Reliability"Now, highlight "Reliability", right-click in the white space to the right and click "New">>"DWORD".Rename it to "ShutdownReasonOn".Click "View" at the top of the editor and then "Refresh".Close the Registry Editor and reboot Server1. Notice that when you reboot Server1 you are no longer asked to provide a reason as to why the server is shutting down. But why exactly did that happen?Log back into Server1 and navigate back to your "ShutdownReasonOn" key. Double-click it and notice its "value" data. It is set to "0". You will learn about binary and hex and decimal values in another course but that "0" value means that the key is turned off. So we added a key that specifies to turn off the functionality that asks the user why they are shutting down the server. If we were to change that value to "1" we would turn that key on and the server would once again begin asking the user for reasons when shutting down.  Screenshot 8: Take a screenshot showing your ShutdownReasonOn key and its value data.

searchDocs.title: Lab 6 Notes​
searchDocs.content: Windows PowerShell is an updated, more powerful version of the command line. It is essentially a combination of a Windows Command Line and a scripting environment rolled into one. It can help with repetitive tasks, processes acting on many files at once, automating and scheduling tasks, and configuring Windows components and services.  While PowerShell is a command line interface, it is more powerful and flexible than the traditional Windows Command Line. It supports complex decision making, connecting to a wide variety of data sources, and can even be used when building graphical user interfaces.  PowerShell is now an essential skill for IT and server administrators. Windows IT professionals who only use a GUI interface for server and network management will still need to know how to use PowerShell as it is by far the most efficient method to accomplish many tasks. It is constantly being developed and there are hundreds of commands.  PowerShell uses commands called CMDLETS (pronounced command-lets). They are English-like commands and use a VERB-NOUN format. It is easy for Linux and Windows Command Line users to get a quick start with PowerShell because of built-in aliases and syntax that is easy to pick up on the fly.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Customizing a Shortcut to Point to a Home Directory​
searchDocs.content: In this exercise we will configure the Powershell Console to open in a directory called “MyScripts.” We will be doing everything on Server1.  To open Powershell, type Powershell from the Run command, or click the Powershell icon on the task bar.First, let's create our new directory. Enter the following command:  New-Item C:\MyScripts -type directory   You should see a message appear confirming the creation of the new directory.  Now create 3 files in that directory:  New-Item C:\MyScripts\file1.txt -type file New-Item C:\MyScripts\file2.txt -type file New-Item C:\MyScripts\file3.txt -type file   Again, you should see confirmation of your commands successfully running.  Now let's create a special shortcut on our desktop that we can use to open Powershell in a specific directory. Navigate to your desktop.Click the blue Windows icon at the bottom of the screen. You should see a "Windows Powershell" icon. If you don't, type in "Powershell" and it will appear.Right-click the "Powershell" icon and click on "Open file location". A window will appear that contains two "Powershell" icons.Right-click the icon that doesn't have the (x86) in its name and click "Properties". A window with a few fields will appear. Look for the "Target:" field.Copy the contents of the "Target:" field.Close the last two windows you opened so that you can see your desktop. Right click anywhere on the desktop that is empty and click on "New" > "Shortcut". The "Create Shortcut" window will appear.Paste what you copied from the "Target:" field in step 8 into the window and click "Next".Rename the shortcut "MyPowershell" and click "Finish". Your new shortcut should now appear on your desktop.Right-click your new shortcut and click on "Properties".Replace the "Start in" field with the path to your "MyScripts" directory: C:\MyScriptsClick "Apply" and then "OK".Now launch Powershell using your newly created shortcut. You should find that when it launches, the command line shows that you are located in your C:\MyScripts directory.You can further customize your Powershell experience. Notice the small downward facing arrow at the top of the Powershell window (right next to the +). Click that arrow and then click "Settings". There are several ways you can customize the way your Powershell terminal looks and behaves here. Feel free to change anything you like before moving forward.  Screenshot 1: Take a screenshot showing that your Powershell terminal opens to the C:\MyScripts directory

searchDocs.title: Investigation 2: Using Powershell CMDLETs​
searchDocs.content: PowerShell commands have been standardized using a “verb-noun” naming convention known as a cmdlet. This standard simplifies the learning curve and provides a description of what the CMDLET does.  Let's try a few basics.  To see a list of CMDLETs available in PowerShell enter the following cmdlet:  get-command   Unfortunately, this command will output a lot of information so we would have to scroll all the way back up to see it all.  Let's try that again but using "more" to make the output more manageable:  get-command | more   That will allow us to scroll through the output more cleanly. (You can hit "q" while in the list to get back to the prompt)  Next, let's list all the commands that use a specific verb, such as "Get". Enter the following:  get-command -Verb Get   Again, you can pipe to "more" to make the output more manageable if you like.  You can use the previous two examples to find any CMDLET that exists on your system.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Getting Help​
searchDocs.content: The "Help" CMDLET noun is very useful in retrieving information about particular CMDLETs.  To begin, enter the following:  get-help   Scroll through the output. Notice the part where it mentions downloading and installing help files.  Our system may not be fully updated with all available CMDLETs and associated help files. Let's take care of that now.  Close the Powershell windowRight-click your Powershell shortcut on the desktop and click "Run as administrator"Now enter the following into Powershell:  Update-Help   Powershell will likely have a lot to update so be patient and let it do its thing. You may get an error at the end of the update mentioning "UI culture(s)". If that is the only error you get, you can safely ignore it.  Now that our Powershell help files are up to date let's take a look at a few.  In Powershell, enter:  Get-Help Get-Childitem   The output will display syntax usage, a description, and related information for the command. The "Get-Help" CMDLET is a useful tool when you are getting started with a CMDLET you haven't used yet.  You can also use this CMDLET with aliases. Try:  Get-Help dir   Notice that the output of this command shows you the same thing as when we ran "Get-Help" with "Get-Childitem". That is because "dir" is an alias of "Get-Childitem". We will come back to aliases later in this lab.  Next, try:  Get-Help Get-Childitem -Full   This outputs a MUCH more detailed help page for the CMDLET. If you look around in it you will also find that it lists the built-in aliases for the CMDLET in the "NOTES" section (in this case "ls", "dir" and "gci"). This is useful to remember for longer CMDLETS.  You can also get some examples of the CMDLET being used with:  Get-Help Get-Childitem -Examples   These are included in the output when using the "-Full" option as well but this option gives you less to scroll through.  Let's try one more:  Get-Help Get-Childitem -Online   Your default web browser should open and bring you to the official Microsoft page for that CMDLET.  In the next section you will be using CMDLETs to manage services on Server1. Use "Get-Help" to learn about the the CMDLETs you will be using:  Get-Help Get-Service Get-Help Start-Service Get-Help Stop-Service

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Using CMDLETs to Start and Stop Services​
searchDocs.content: There are several CMDLETs associates with the "Service" noun:  Get-ServiceNew-ServiceRestart-ServiceSet-ServiceStart-ServiceStop-ServiceSuspend-Service  We are going to use a few of these with a simple service but first let's take a look at the services available on our computer with:  Get-Service   You will see a list of all the services available on Server1 and their status.  We can get service information for a specific service with the "-name" option:  Get-Service -name Spooler   Notice that the Spooler service is currently running. Let's stop it:  Stop-Service -name Spooler   Now, check its status again:  Get-Service -name Spooler   You should see the status has changed from "Running" to "Stopped".  Screenshot 2: Take a screenshot showing that the Spooler service is stopped  Before we move on, start it back up again:  Start-Service -name Spooler   Screenshot 3: Take a screenshot showing that the Spooler service is Running

searchDocs.title: Investigation 3: Aliases​
searchDocs.content: Aliases are strings that reference CMDLETs. Powershell has several built-in aliases (including many Linux commands) to make it easier for people to get started with Powershell, even if they are used to different operating system.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Finding Built-In Aliases​
searchDocs.content: You have already seen a few of these earlier in the lab (the aliases for Get-Childitem). There are a couple CMDLETs that are useful when looking for existing aliases.  In Powershell, enter:  Get-Alias   The output of this CMDLET will show you a list of aliases on the left and what CMDLET they reference on the right.  You can also check specific CMDLETs for what aliases they have. Try:  Get-Alias -Definition Get-Childtem   You should get a listing of all the aliases associated with the "Get-Childitem" CMDLET. Try running each alias and see what the output looks like. They should all be the same.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: User-Defined Aliases​
searchDocs.content: While the built-in aliases are useful, the real power in aliases comes from the ability to create our own. You can add however many aliases for however many CMDLETs you'd like to better suit your environment or administration style.  However, user-defined aliases are not permanent. They exists as long as the Powershell session is active and are removed when the session is closed. Before we get around that problem, let's test it out to see what happens.  Run the following in Powershell:  Set-Alias gs Get-Service   Now run the alias you just set:  gs   You should get the output of the "Get-Service" CMDLET.  Now try:  gs -name Spooler   You should get the status of the Spooler service.  Screenshot 4: Take a screenshot showing the Spooler status output coming from the "gs" alias  Now, close Powershell, open it again, and try running your "gs" alias again. What happened? You should be met with an error. Add the alias again:  Set-Alias gs Get-Service   Now run:  Get-Alias -Name gs   This will show you what CMDLET the "gs" alias is mapped to.  Screenshot 5: Take a screenshot showing the "gs" alias mapped to the "Get-Service" CMDLET.  There are a few reasons why aliases are not permanent. In particular, we don't want old aliases hanging around when we start scripting as they can cause problems if we don't know they are there or if we forget what aliases have been set.  There is a way to make them permanent if we want to, however...

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Creating a Profile​
searchDocs.content: You can create a PowerShell profile to customize your environment and to add session-specific elements to every PowerShell session that you start.  A PowerShell profile is a script that runs when PowerShell starts. You can use the profile as a logon script to customize the environment. You can add commands, aliases, functions, variables, snap-ins, modules, and PowerShell drives.  We are going to stick to a simple example here but Powershell Profiles are extremely useful to administrators because you can tailor Powershell sessions to your specific local and network environment.  "$PROFILE" is a special system variable that references a file representing the users specific Powershell startup script.  In Powershell run:  $PROFILE   You should get a file path pointing to your current profile.  Try to edit this file with:  Notepad $Profile   You should be met with an error. Click "OK" and then close the Notepad window. You received an error because no profile actually exists yet. Let's create one.  Enter the following command:  New-Item -Itemtype File -Path $Profile -Force   You should receive output showing that the file has been created.  Now let's try opening it again:  Notepad $Profile   An empty file should open up.  Let's add our "gs" alias to it. Enter the following into the file:  Set-Alias gs Get-Service   Save the file and close it.  Close Powershell and open it again.Try running:  gs -name Spooler   Your alias should be working.  Run:  type $profile   This will give you the contents of your profile file.  Screenshot 6: Take a screenshot of the output of "type $profile" which should have your alias entry.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 1: Importing Modules​
searchDocs.content: We can use Powershell to add features just like we do with the Server Manager. In fact, you already did this back in lab 3 on Server2 (when you added and removed Print Services).

searchDocs.title: Part 1: Adding a New Feature​
searchDocs.content: Let's try adding Hyper-V to Server1.  In Powershell enter the following:  Add-WindowsFeature Hyper-V-Tools   Once that finished installing, enter the following:  Add-WindowsFeature Hyper-V-Powershell   You should get "Success" confirmation messages for both installations.  Screenshot 1: Take a screenshot showing the two Hyper-V features were added successfully.  Now that we have our new features installed, we can move on to its modules.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Importing a Module for our New Feature​
searchDocs.content: A module is a package that contains PowerShell commands, such as CMDLETs, providers, functions, workflows, variables, and aliases.  People who write commands can use modules to organize their commands and share them with others.  After a module is imported, you can use the module members in your session.  Some modules come pre-imported (installed). Some modules are on the server but need to be installed before you are able to use the CMDLETs and function in them.  To find the modules that have already been imported into your session, at the PowerShell prompt, type:  Get-Module   You can also get a listing of modules that are installed but not yet imported into your session:  Get-Module -ListAvailable   To import a module we use the "Import-Module" CMDLET. Let's add the Hyper-V module:  Import-Module Hyper-V   If the CMDLET works, you should get no output.  Now let's see what that module added:  Get-Command -Module Hyper-V   You should be met with a list of all the CMDLETs that the Hyper-V module added to Powershell.  Screenshot 2: Take a screenshot showing the output of "Get-Command -Module Hyper-V".  Remember you can always use the "Get-Help" CMDLET for help with new CMDLETS but you will probably have to update your help files:  Update-Help   You can ignore any errors. Then:  Get-Help New-VM   Now generally there is no point in removing modules since they are lost once you close the session but you can technically do so manually with:  Remove-Module Hyper-V

searchDocs.title: Investigation 2: Creating a Function​
searchDocs.content: A function is a list of Powershell statements that has a name that you assign. When you run a function, you type the function name. The statements in the list run as if you had typed them at the command prompt. It is like a mini-script or a complex CMDLET or alias with parameters and options.  We will create two simple functions.  Begin by closing all Powershell windows if you have any open.Next, right-click the MyPowershell shortcut on your desktop and click "Run as administrator".Enter the following:  Function Start-PSAdmin {Start-Process PowerShell -Verb RunAs}   Now try running your new function:  Start-PSAdmin   A new PowerShell window should appear.  Screenshot 3: Take a screenshot showing what happens when you run "Start-PSAdmin".  Now let's try something with a bit of utility. We are going to add a multi-line function called "Get-SmallFiles". This function has a user-defined variable called "$size". This function displays all the files that are smaller than the user-defined variable and excludes directories.  At the PS prompt, enter:  Function Get-SmallFiles { Param($Size) Get-ChildItem | Where-Object { $_.Length -lt $Size -and !$_.PSIsContainer } }   Note - as you enter this into PowerShell, the "{" and "}" special characters will allow you to use multiple lines for the function. You also do not need to worry about spacing or tabs. PowerShell will take care of that for you as well.  Before we run this function, let's take a step to help show that it works. We already have 3 empty files in our "MyScripts" directory. Let's add another file that has something in it. Run:  Copy-Item -Path "C:\Windows\iis.log" -Destination "C:\MyScripts\iiscopy.txt"   Now, make sure you are in your "MyScripts" directory and get a listing of its contents (You should know a few ways to do this now!) and note what the output is. Finally, run your function for files smaller than 50 bits:  Get-SmallFiles -Size 50   Notice the difference in output. Your function is only returning the empty files because they are smaller than the specified size.  Screenshot 4: Take a screenshot showing the output of "Get-SmallFiles -Size 50".

searchDocs.title: Investigation 3: Updating Profile with Modules and Functions​
searchDocs.content: The problem with the modules and functions we've added and used in this lab is that they disappear when we close our PowerShell session. However, just like an Alias, we can put these into our Profile so that they are available whenever we open a new session.  Run:  Notepad $profile   Inside the file, add the module import and functions you have done so far in this lab:  Import-Module Hyper-V Function Start-PSAdmin {Start-Process PowerShell -Verb RunAs} function Get-SmallFiles { Param($Size) Get-ChildItem | Where-Object { $_.Length -lt $Size -and !$_.PSIsContainer } }   Note - Unlike when you first created the "Get-SmallFiles" function, the tab spacing will not be done automatically for you in the "$Profile" file. For clarity, the first line has 0 tabs, the second and third line have 1 tab, the fourth line has 2 tabs, the fifth line has 1 tab, and the last line has 0 tabs.  Screenshot 5: Take a screenshot showing the contents of your "$Profile" file.  Save your file and close it. Also, close your PowerShell window. Open a new PowerShell window and test to make sure your module import and two functions are working.

searchDocs.title: Investigation 4: Introduction to PowerShell Scripting​
searchDocs.content: Scripting is an integral part of being any kind of administrator. Scripts will make your life easier and will allow you to automate many tasks and process all sorts of system and network based information.  That said, the idea of scripting and how it is used in practice is entirely dependant on who is using it and all kinds of other factors surrounding your local and network environment, security policies, goals of your company, and just so much more.  It is a wide and deep ocean of which PowerShell is only a small part. It is unlikely that you will become a scripting expert of any kind doing solely what is taught to you in this course or any other courses you take.  You will not learn all that much from slides and lectures. You need to actually do scripting.  In this course/lab we are going to just barely scratch the surface of PowerShell scripting. This may seem daunting (and it is) but you will come to better understand scripting and how to effectively write and use scripts the more your write and use scripts.  And remember, being bad at something is just the first step towards being kinda ok at something.

searchDocs.title: Part 1: PowerShell ISE​
searchDocs.content: Before we actually get into scripting, you should be introduced to PowerShell ISE (Integrated Scripting Environment). ISE is basically a text editor and PowerShell terminal in one application that has many useful features and tools for scripting and testing of scripts.  Let's open it up.  Click the Windows icon and type "PowerShell".Click on "Windows PowerShell ISE". The application will open and it will look similar to a standard PowerShell terminal but you will notice many other buttons and tools available.  Notice on the right hand side there is a list of CMDLETs. You can type into the "Name" field at the top to search for specific ones and you can further refine your search by changing the "Modules" dropdown to a specific module (like Hyper-V for example).  You can use the main PowerShell terminal in the middle as normal.  Use it to navigate to your "MyScripts" directory with the following:  cd c:\MyScripts   Notice that as you do so, PowerShell ISE will give you an auto-fill option for your directory. This is called "Intellisense" and it will recommend how to finish your commands. You can hit the "Tab" key on your keyboard to accept a suggestion.  Now let's open the Script Pane. Click on "View" > "Show Script Pane".  Your PowerShell ISE window will be split in two, with the PowerShell terminal below and the newly visible Script Pane above.  The Script Pane allows us to create scripts but it also has a neat feature in that it allows us to run CMDLETs, scripts, or parts of scripts for testing without actually saving a script file.  Enter the following in the Script Pane:  Get-Date Get-ChildItem   Find the green "Run Script" arrow above the Script Pane and click it. Notice what happens. The entries for the script you are writing above are processed and their output appears in the PowerShell terminal below. This is super useful when we are creating scripts because it allows us to test chunks of our script without needing an entire one. Close PowerShell ISE. Click "No" when asked it you want to save changes.

searchDocs.title: Part 2: Using Variables​
searchDocs.content: In the context of scripting, a variable is a string that contains a value. What that value is will depend on how the variable is created and what is stored in it.  Let's try creating a simple variable, storing a value in it, and then recalling that value.  Open PowerShell ISE. The Script Pane should open as well. Open it if it does not.Enter the following into the Script Pane:  $name= Read-Host "What is your name?"   Click the green "Run Script" arrow above the Script Pane and take a look at the PowerShell terminal (with the blue background). You should see that you are being asked for your name.Enter your name in the PowerShell terminal and hit "Enter". What happened?Now, in the PowerShell terminal, enter the following:  echo $name   You should see your name appear. What we have just done is stored a value in a variable called "name", denoted by the ($) in front of it. That special symbol in front of a string tells us that it is a variable. Variables are very useful in scripting because it allows us to apply sets of instructions to all sorts of inputs depending on what we want our script to do.  Let's enhance our script a bit using another variable.  First, let's actually save our script so we can access it later. In PowerShell ISE, click "File" and then "Save As". Name your script "MyFirstScript" and save it in your "MyScripts" directory.Now, below the line asking for a name, add the following to your script:  $age= Read-Host "How old are you?"   Click the green "Run Script" arrow above the Script Pane. You will get a message stating the script you are about to run will be saved. Click "OK" and take a look at the PowerShell terminal below. Answer the two questions.In the PowerShell terminal, enter the following:  echo $name echo $age   We have now stored two variables: the "name" variable and the "age" variable. To do this we used the "Read-Host" CMDLET. This allows us to ask the user to input a string of data which is captured and stored in the variables we specified. Now that we have these variable full of data we can actually do something with them. The simplest way to use the data is to write it back out to the screen. To do that we will use the "Write-Host" CMDLET.  Back in the Script Pane, enter this next line into your script and then click the green "Run Script" arrow:  Write-Host "Hello $name. Welcome to $env:COMPUTERNAME"   Notice that your script now has output. We captured the user's input and wrote it back out to them using the "name" variable we created. We also used what's called an "Environment Variable", something that is baked in to all instances of Powershell. In this case we used the "COMPUTERNAME" environment variable which pulls the name of our computer and we injected that into the output of our script. But what about that "age" variable? We are going to use that to learn about conditional logic.

searchDocs.title: Part 3: Conditional Logic​
searchDocs.content: Conditional logic is the foundation on which most scripting operates. There are many types of conditional logic but we are going to focus on the most basic: If Statements.  If statements allow us to test conditions and take different actions based on what the result of that test is. In this next step, we are going to test against our "age" variable and output different messages to the user based on what age they enter.  Begin by adding these next few lines to your script:  if ($age -lt 30) {Write-Host "You are young."} if ($age -gt 30) {Write-Host "You are old."}   Click the green "Run Script" arrow. When the script runs, enter your name as usual and enter "20" for the age. Notice the output.Test run the script again, this time entering "40" for the age. Notice the output.  Depending on what number you enter for the "age" variable, you will get a different output. There are a few problems with this logic, however.  Test run the script again. This time, when it asks for your age enter "Banana". What happens?  The script will likely output "You are old." even though you did not enter a number.  Now try running it again. This time, when it asks for your age enter "30". What happens?  You will likely not receive any output for the age question because the number you entered is neither greater than or less than 30.  This is a problem. We have not accounted for invalid data input by the user.  In our current example, accounting for invalid user data is fairly simple. Let's begin by fixing the easier issue.  Change the current line in your script:  if ($age -gt 30) {Write-Host "You are old."}   to  if ($age -ge 30) {Write-Host "You are old."}   Now test run the script again, entering "30" for the age. Notice that now the script gives an output for that number.  To fix the issue of the user not giving us a valid number, there are two things we have to worry about here. First, we don't want the user to give us something that isn't a number. Second, we don't want the user giving us a negative number since people can't be "negative" years old. To accomplish this, we are going to use "elseif" and "else" to restructure our script a little.  Replace your two if statement lines with the following:  if ($age -notmatch '^\d+$') { Write-Host "Please enter a valid non-negative number." } elseif ([int]$age -lt 30) { Write-Host "You are young." } else { Write-Host "You are old." }   We have changed a few things here in our conditional logic to ensure that the user can ONLY give us valid and usable data.  Take a look at the first if statement:  if ($age -notmatch '^\d+$') { Write-Host "Please enter a valid non-negative number." }   This tests to see if the user entered a regular number. It does this using the "-nomatch" flag and something called a "regular expression". You will learn more about these in your OPS145 class. This particular regular expression essentially matches only a string that begins with (^) and ends with ($) a number (\d) or a set of numbers (+). This condition isn't perfect because it will match any regular number (635819 would be acceptable for example) so it won't disallow ages that are wildly unrealistic but for the purposes of our script it works nicely. If the user gives us anything else, a message is sent back to tell them their input was not valid.  The next condition is pretty much the same as our original if statements:  elseif ([int]$age -lt 30) { Write-Host "You are young." }   The difference here is that we are using "elseif" instead of just "if" so the logic only processes if the first condition fails. The "[int]" ensures that whatever is stored in the "age" variable is converted to an integer. This isn't necessary in our example but it is a good idea when working with numbers.  Finally we have:  else { Write-Host "You are old." }   Using "else" is the same as saying "if none of the above conditional statements succeeded, do this". Since we have two conditional statements that cover invalid inputs and any number under 30, all that's left are numbers over 30 and so we can safely attach our "You are old." message to the "else" since we know that if the script gets to this point, the user must have input a number of 30 or higher.  Test run your script to see the differences in output.  We can also expand on what conditions we are applying to our logic.  Change your conditions to match the following:  if ($age -notmatch '^\d+$') { Write-Host "Please enter a valid non-negative number." } elseif ([int]$age -lt 30) { Write-Host "You are young." } elseif ([int]$age -ge 30 -and [int]$age -lt 60) { Write-Host "You are old." } else { Write-Host "Oh wow, you are ANCIENT!" }   Test run your script 3 more times, using 10, 40, and 70 for the ages and notice the different outputs.  We now have a functioning script that uses variables and conditional logic to output a few different pieces of information. However, we have skipped one of the most important parts of scripting: comments.  Comments are important because they explain each part of our script. This is useful for us as the script creator for when we walk away from a partially completed script to come back to it later but also in case someone else wants to use our script. The comments ensure anyone looking through it understands what the script is meant to do and how it works. So let's clean up our script. We will also add in a date capture while we are at it.  Change your entire script to:  #Script Purpose: Gather users name and age. Output user's name and computer name and a message based on age entered #Author: Your Name (replace with your actual name) #Date Created: Today's Date (Enter the actual date) #Ask the user for their name and then store their input in a variable $name= Read-Host "What is your name?" #Ask the user for their age and then store their input in a variable $age= Read-Host "How old are you?" #Insert an empty line to clean up output Write-Host "" #Output a message to the user saying hello to them and welcoming them to the current computer Write-Host "Hello $name. Welcome to $env:COMPUTERNAME" #Insert an empty line to clean up output Write-Host "" #Store the current date in a variable and then use it to tell the user the current date $date= Get-Date -Format D Write-Host "The current date is: $date" #Insert an empty line to clean up output Write-Host "" #Test the user's age and output an appropriate message based on how old they are (or ask them to provide valid data if they did not) if ($age -notmatch '^\d+$') { Write-Host "Please enter a valid non-negative number." } elseif ([int]$age -lt 30) { Write-Host "You are young." } elseif ([int]$age -ge 30 -and [int]$age -lt 60) { Write-Host "You are old." } else { Write-Host "Oh wow, you are ANCIENT!" }   SET EXECUTION POLICY
